lead: A thyristor, or silicon controlled rectifier (SCR), is a four-layer p-n-p-n switch with anode, cathode and gate. With the anode negative it blocks whatever the gate does. With the anode positive it blocks until a small gate current turns it on; then it latches and needs no gate current. It turns off only when the circuit brings its current to zero. Two internal transistors that drive each other explain the latch. SCRs switch large power in controlled rectifiers, AC voltage controllers, battery chargers and HVDC links.
prereq: You need: the bipolar transistor and its current gain, and the power diode of the first chapter.

blocks.text: An SCR is one silicon wafer with four layers P1, N1, P2 and N2. P1 is the anode A, N2 the cathode K, and the gate G is a contact on P2 near the cathode. The layers form three junctions: J1 (P1-N1), J2 (N1-P2) and J3 (P2-N2). N1 is the wide, lightly doped layer that holds the blocking voltage.

Anode positive, no gate current: J1 and J3 are forward biased but J2 is reverse biased, so only a small leakage current flows. This is the forward blocking state. Anode negative: J1 and J3 are reverse biased and the device is in reverse blocking. A gate pulse cannot turn it on in this state, and a gate current applied with the anode negative only increases the reverse leakage and heats the device, so the gate is not driven then.
Plot the anode current I<sub>A</sub> against the anode-cathode voltage V<sub>AK</sub>. The characteristic has three regions.

items: Reverse blocking (V<sub>AK</sub> negative): a small leakage current until the reverse breakdown voltage V<sub>BR</sub>, which damages the device.

Forward blocking (V<sub>AK</sub> positive, device off): a small leakage current until the forward breakover voltage V<sub>BO</sub>. With I<sub>G</sub> = 0, at V<sub>BO</sub> junction J2 breaks down and the device switches on by itself. A larger gate current lowers the breakover voltage.
Forward conduction (on): a steep line at a low drop of about 1 V to 2 V. The load and the supply, not the SCR, set the current.

blocks.text: Two anode currents describe the latch. The latching current I<sub>L</sub> is the minimum anode current that must be reached while the gate pulse is still present, so that the SCR stays on when the pulse ends. The holding current I<sub>H</sub> is the minimum anode current that keeps an SCR that is already on in conduction; below I<sub>H</sub> it turns off. I<sub>L</sub> is larger than I<sub>H</sub>, often two to three times. Both are anode currents, not gate ratings.

Cut the four layers diagonally into two transistors that share the middle layers. T1 is p-n-p (P1-N1-P2): emitter at the anode. T2 is n-p-n (N1-P2-N2): emitter at the cathode, base at the gate. The collector of T1 feeds the base of T2, and the collector of T2 feeds the base of T1. Each transistor supplies the other's base current; this loop is called regeneration.

Let α₁ and α₂ be the common-base current gains of T1 and T2, and I<sub>CBO1</sub>, I<sub>CBO2</sub> their leakage currents. T1 collector current is α₁I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>CBO1</sub> and T2 collector current is α₂I<sub>K</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub>. Their sum is the anode current, and I<sub>K</sub> = I<sub>A</sub> + I<sub>G</sub>. Solving gives the anode current:
where I<sub>A</sub> is the anode current, I<sub>G</sub> the gate current, α₁ and α₂ the common-base gains and I<sub>CBO1</sub>, I<sub>CBO2</sub> the leakage currents, all currents in amperes.

In silicon transistors α rises with current. At low current α₁ + α₂ is well below 1 and I<sub>A</sub> is small: the device blocks. Gate current raises the current, both α values rise, the denominator shrinks, and when α₁ + α₂ reaches 1 the loop sustains itself and only the external circuit limits I<sub>A</sub>. The SCR has latched; removing the gate current changes nothing.

examples.question: In the two-transistor model of an SCR, I<sub>G</sub> = 20 mA and I<sub>CBO1</sub> + I<sub>CBO2</sub> = 10 µA. (a) At low current α₁ = 0.40 and α₂ = 0.45; find I<sub>A</sub>. (b) As the current grows the gains become α₁ = 0.48 and α₂ = 0.50; find I<sub>A</sub> again. (c) What happens when α₁ + α₂ reaches 1 in a circuit of 200 V and 20 Ω?
steps: I<sub>A</sub> = 0.010 01 ÷ 0.02 = 0.50 A: the same gate current now gives eight times as much anode current.
(c) At α₁ + α₂ = 1 the denominator is zero: the device latches and the circuit sets the current, I<sub>A</sub> ≈ 200 V ÷ 20 Ω = 10 A.
examples.answer: I<sub>A</sub> = 60.1 mA, then 0.50 A; at α₁ + α₂ = 1 the SCR latches and carries about 10 A set by the load.

examples.question: An SCR with latching current I<sub>L</sub> = 50 mA feeds a load of R = 20 Ω and L = 0.5 H from a 100 V DC supply. Find the minimum width of the gate pulse.
steps: After turn-on the current rises as i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−Rt/L</sup>), with V/R = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 A and L/R = 0.5 ÷ 20 = 0.025 s.
The gate must stay on until i reaches I<sub>L</sub>: 0.05 = 5 (1 − e<sup>−t/0.025</sup>), so e<sup>−t/0.025</sup> = 0.99.
examples.answer: The gate pulse must last at least about 251 µs; with a 10 µs pulse this SCR would turn off again when the pulse ends.

traps: The gate cannot turn an SCR off. Removing the gate pulse after latching does nothing; turn-off needs the anode current below I<sub>H</sub> and reverse bias for long enough (commutation).
I<sub>L</sub> is larger than I<sub>H</sub>, not the other way round. Both are anode currents.
V<sub>BO</sub> (forward breakover, the device turns on) is not V<sub>BR</sub> (reverse breakdown, the device is damaged).
Drawing the SCR on in the third quadrant: the conduction branch is only in the first quadrant (V<sub>AK</sub> and I<sub>A</sub> positive).

quiz.q: Name the four layers of an SCR from anode to cathode, its three junctions and its three terminals.
quiz.a: P1, N1, P2, N2; junctions J1 (P1-N1), J2 (N1-P2), J3 (P2-N2); terminals anode, cathode and gate (on P2).

quiz.q: Define latching current and holding current, and say which is larger.
quiz.a: I<sub>L</sub>: the minimum anode current that must flow while the gate pulse is present for the SCR to stay on after the pulse ends. I<sub>H</sub>: the minimum anode current that keeps a conducting SCR on. I<sub>L</sub> > I<sub>H</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does an SCR block current when its anode is positive and no gate current flows?
quiz.a: J1 and J3 are forward biased but the middle junction J2 is reverse biased. J2 holds the voltage, so only leakage current flows until V<sub>BO</sub>.

quiz.q: With I<sub>G</sub> = 30 mA, α₂ = 0.4, α₁ = 0.5 and negligible leakage, find I<sub>A</sub> from the two-transistor model.
An SCR with I<sub>L</sub> = 40 mA supplies R = 10 Ω, L = 0.1 H from 200 V DC. Find the minimum gate pulse width.
An SCR has V<sub>BO</sub> = 600 V with the gate open, yet a gate pulse turns it on at V<sub>AK</sub> = 200 V. Explain why this does not contradict the meaning of V<sub>BO</sub>.
quiz.a: V<sub>BO</sub> is the breakover voltage with zero gate current. Gate current adds base current to the n-p-n part, raising α₁ + α₂ towards 1 at a lower anode voltage, so the device latches below V<sub>BO</sub>. That is normal gate control.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phase-control thyristors are still made for several kilovolts and thousands of amperes, and line-commutated HVDC converters use long strings of them because their on-state loss is low and they are robust. The integrated gate-commutated thyristor (IGCT) keeps the thyristor's low conduction drop but can be turned off from the gate. Search for ‘phase control thyristor datasheet’ and ‘line-commutated converter HVDC’.

figure.caption: Static V–I characteristic of an SCR (a sketch, not to scale). Gate current lowers the breakover voltage; once the anode current passes the latching current the device stays on the steep conduction line.
